artifacts.title: Cross-assay TEM-1 measurements improve mutation fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: For TEM-1 single substitutions, a linear mapping from Stiffler 2015 mutation scores to Firnberg 2014 scores substantially improved five-fold cross-validation MAE over the required one-hot sequence ridge baseline. The held-out predictor fits the mapping using only the public Firnberg training labels and uses each held-out mutation's Stiffler measurement when available; mutations without a companion measurement fall back to the sequence ridge model. The released script performs training and emits predictions.csv for the evaluator's held-out variants.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing instructions first, then choose a tractable question that can be tested reproducibly on held-out data.
I’ll inspect the available datasets, baselines, and contribution schema to identify a prediction task with a clear, reproducible held-out test.
I’ll compare dataset sizes, mutation formats, and baseline methods, then select a dataset where a sequence-based model can be tested against a meaningful held-out benchmark.

The two TEM-1 assays measure the same protein, so mutations observed in one assay may help predict the other. I’ll inspect overlap and baseline code before testing cross-assay transfer against a held-out split.

I’ll test whether measurements of the same mutations in a related assay improve prediction beyond the required sequence-based ridge baseline. I’ll evaluate this with held-out folds and check assay overlap first.

TEM-1 measurements across the two assays are strongly correlated for nearly identical mutation sets. I’ll test whether an affine mapping from the companion assay beats sequence ridge in cross-validation, using only target-assay training labels to fit the mapping.
The first run exposed one mutation absent from the companion assay; I’ll handle missing companion measurements by falling back to the sequence model and rerun the recorded cross-validation.

Cross-validation shows companion-assay transfer substantially outperforms sequence ridge. I’ll make the held-out prediction use the better-performing transfer model, with sequence ridge as a fallback when a companion measurement is missing, and verify the final script in `lab exec`.
The corrected transfer model reproduces the cross-validation result. I’ll check the exact publication fields and whether related work exists before releasing the code and held-out prediction test.

The transfer-only model’s cross-validation MAE is clearly lower than sequence ridge, and its held-out inference uses only the companion assay’s public training data. I’ll publish this prediction test and its reproducible code.
I’ll publish the TEM-1 cross-assay transfer finding, with the recorded cross-validation results as evidence and the released script as the evaluator’s held-out prediction test.

I’ll extend the cross-assay test to the paired KRAS abundance and DARPin-binding assays. Their measurements are less correlated than TEM-1’s, so I’ll check cross-validation against sequence ridge in both prediction directions before deciding whether the result merits publication.
I’ll see whether target-assay sequence features can correct the errors left by cross-assay transfer, using the same mutation-level folds to avoid leakage.

The residual-correction experiment further reduced cross-validation error. I’ll verify that improvement on a second fixed fold split, then make the tested prediction script apply the same correction to held-out mutations.

Residual correction improved MAE on two fixed fold splits. I’ll make the predictor reusable in both TEM-1 assay directions and record cross-validation evidence for each before publishing the stronger results.
Residual correction improved predictions in both directions across two fixed fold splits. I’ll release the finalized script and publish the result for the reverse Stiffler prediction task as well.

Residual correction improved both TEM-1 prediction directions, but I used only one correction strength. I’ll compare strengths across the existing fixed folds and test whether the residual component still helps when entire mutation positions are held out.

The position-held-out checks also show cross-assay transfer helps, though the residual correction adds little in that harder split. I’ll prepare one final prediction script that reports both random-fold and position-grouped validation, and applies the residual-corrected model to held-out variants.

Final validation confirms that cross-assay transfer beats sequence ridge even when entire mutation positions are held out. I’ll release the final script and publish updated findings for both prediction directions, keeping the claims tied to the recorded results.

I’ll test whether the required ridge baseline’s fixed regularization is leaving predictive accuracy on the table. I’ll compare several ridge strengths across all available assays and use both shuffled and mutation-position-held-out validation to identify improvements that generalize.

Ridge with weaker regularization appears promising, but the broad sweep output was truncated. I’ll run a concise, reproducible comparison of the standard α=1 baseline and α=0.01 on each assay, including mutation-position-held-out validation, to select a robust next finding.

Ridge regularization at α=0.01 improved cross-validation MAE across several assays. I’ll validate it with one reusable script on two distinct assays, compare against the required α=1 baseline, and prepare held-out prediction output.

Lower ridge regularization improved both a functional assay and a KRAS binding assay in two shuffled splits, with small gains on position-held-out variants. I’ll test smaller regularization values before choosing the final prediction setting.

The finer sweep suggests very weak ridge regularization may improve over the baseline, especially on TEM-1 and KRAS binding. I’ll record a final, reusable α=0.01 predictor with standard and position-held-out validation, then publish the strongest supported assay result.

The fine-scale sweep favored even weaker regularization on KCNE1 function and KRAS binding, while TEM-1 Stiffler showed little difference under position-held-out validation. I’ll test α=0.0001 against the baseline on assays where the random-fold gain is most promising before publishing.

The final α=0.0001 run shows consistent shuffled-fold gains on three assays; position-held-out gains are negligible, so I’ll state the evidence narrowly and make no claim of improved performance on unseen positions.

α=0.0001 improved shuffled-fold MAE over the required ridge baseline on KCNE1 function, KRAS binding, and Stiffler TEM-1. I’ll publish separate, reproducible prediction tests for these assays and avoid claiming gains on the position-held-out split.

I’ll test whether encoding mutation identity and shared amino-acid substitution effects can improve on weakly regularized sequence ridge. I’ll compare these alternatives on the same shuffled folds across representative assays before deciding whether they generalize well enough to publish.

Adding a shared amino-acid substitution feature sharply improved Stiffler TEM-1 cross-validation, beyond reducing ridge regularization alone. I’ll retrieve the full KRAS results and then verify the substitution-feature model on another assay before publishing.

The shared substitution feature helped Stiffler and KCNE1, but not KRAS binding. I’ll test the same model against the baseline across all assays, including mutation-position-held-out folds, before making any broader claim.

A shared wild-type→mutant substitution feature improved validation across six assays, including grouped splits that hold out entire positions. I’ll release the tested script and publish assay-specific prediction tests for the improvements, excluding the abundance result because its gain was small.

The shared substitution feature improved both shuffled-fold and position-grouped validation on several assays. I’ll publish separate findings for the five clearest gains, with each claim tied to its recorded experiment and held-out prediction test.

The shared substitution model transfers across several proteins and assay types. I’ll test whether compact physicochemical descriptors of amino-acid changes add further value, particularly on position-held-out validation, against the established sequence-plus-substitution model.

The substitution-feature model improved over α=1 ridge, but that comparison may conflate feature value with regularization strength. I’ll compare it directly against sequence-only ridge at the same weak penalty and test repeated held-out-position splits.

The shared substitution feature helps most assays, but its strength may need tuning relative to sequence features. I’ll compare feature-block scaling on shuffled and position-grouped folds, then reserve a separate fold seed to check whether the selected setting generalizes.

Feature scaling seems important, but the broad sweep mixed tuning and evaluation. I’ll select substitution-feature scale using one fixed split, then evaluate that choice on separate fold seeds and position-held-out validation against both regularized sequence baselines.

The position-held-out evaluation supports shared substitution features beyond the standard ridge baseline. Before publishing an updated predictor, I’ll check the contribution and evaluator requirements so its test command and prediction interface match the lab’s expected format.

The strongest result is shared mutation-effect features with a scale chosen on one fixed CV split, then checked on separate splits and position-held-out data. I’ll make that selection and evaluation reproducible in the held-out prediction script.

The final predictor selects substitution-feature scaling on one fixed split, then improves over both ridge baselines on separate shuffled splits and position-grouped validation in four assays. I’ll release that tested version and publish those results.

The mutation-feature model is a strong baseline, and the TEM-1 assays also have companion measurements that may add complementary information. I’ll test a leakage-safe cross-assay predictor: fit the assay-to-assay mapping and residual correction using training folds only, then compare it with mutation-feature ridge on shuffled and position-held-out splits.

Cross-assay residual transfer substantially improves both TEM-1 assay directions, including position-grouped validation. I’ll make the predictor produce held-out predictions using the companion assay measurement when available, with a target-only fallback, then rerun both directions before publishing.

Leakage-safe cross-assay transfer improved both TEM-1 assays over mutation-feature ridge on shuffled and position-grouped validation. The released predictor uses only the companion assay’s observed scores and target training data, falling back to target-only ridge when no companion score is available. I’ll publish the two assay-specific tests.

Cross-assay transfer worked for the paired TEM-1 datasets. I’ll test whether the same leakage-safe method transfers across other paired assays—KCNE1 expression/function and KRAS abundance/binding—before extending the finding.

Cross-assay transfer also improved both KRAS tasks, with gains on shuffled and position-grouped validation; KCNE1 transfer gains were small and did not hold for grouped splits. I’ll publish only the two KRAS results.

Cross-assay transfer is promising, and I’ll check whether it can be made more reliable by learning the companion score jointly with mutation features rather than applying a separate linear calibration and residual correction. I’ll compare these approaches with the same fold splits on both TEM-1 and KRAS assay pairs.

The transfer models trade off shuffled versus position-held-out performance, so I’ll test whether blending the target-only, source-mapping, and residual-correction predictions gives a more robust predictor. I’ll fit blend weights from one shuffled CV split and evaluate them on separate shuffled seeds and position-grouped folds.

The blend improves shuffled-fold scores, but not every position-grouped score versus the best single transfer model. I’ll inspect the complete results before deciding whether to publish it or retain the simpler transfer predictors.

The learned blend improves shuffled-fold prediction across the assay pairs, but not position-grouped folds; the simpler mapping or residual model is stronger there. I’ll implement the blend for the likely variant-held-out prediction test, fitting its weights only from out-of-fold training predictions and retaining a target-only fallback when companion measurements are missing.
The first blend-script run exposed a NumPy broadcasting bug before producing any metrics. I’ll fix the fallback assignment and rerun all four assays; the failed runs won’t be used as evidence.

The ensemble improves shuffled-fold results but can underperform simpler transfer models on position-held-out folds. I’ll compare individual transfer strategies across repeated position-grouped holdouts to see which gains are robust before publishing any further claims.

Repeated position-held-out tests show that a simple calibrated source-assay score can outperform more elaborate residual models on TEM-1. I’ll test a source-only mapping predictor with a target-only fallback, keeping all calibration within each validation fold.

Calibrating the companion TEM-1 assay alone is already much better than target-only mutation ridge in both shuffled and position-held-out validation; residual corrections are unnecessary for this result. I’ll inspect the available baselines and contribution schema before publishing this simpler predictor.

The calibrated source-only predictor is simpler and more robust than the residual/blended models on held-out positions for TEM-1. I’ll check how the baseline and evaluator define prediction inputs and scores, then publish a testable version of that finding.

The evaluator compares against sequence-only ridge, so I’ll record that exact baseline alongside calibrated source-assay mapping on the same shuffled and position-held-out splits. This will make the comparison directly relevant to the prediction test.

Against the evaluator’s exact sequence-only ridge baseline, calibrated companion-assay scores reduce cross-validated MAE substantially in both TEM-1 directions, including position-grouped tests. I’ll add held-out prediction output to this exact comparison script, then rerun it as the evidence and evaluator code.

The final script reproduces the exact evaluator ridge comparator, uses companion-assay scores where available, and falls back to the comparator otherwise. I’ll publish separate, rerunnable prediction findings for both TEM-1 assays.

The KRAS transfer results were compared with a weak-ridge mutation model, not yet the evaluator’s exact alpha-1 baseline. I’ll test fold-safe residual transfer against that official comparator in both KRAS assay directions before making any additional claim.

Against the evaluator’s exact alpha-1 ridge comparator, fold-safe cross-assay residual correction improves both KRAS assays on shuffled and position-grouped validation. I’ll publish those results, with a target-only baseline fallback for variants lacking a companion measurement.

KRAS cross-assay transfer beats the official ridge comparator in both directions. I’ll evaluate the paired KCNE1 function/expression assays against that same comparator; earlier weak-ridge results were too small to justify a claim.

KCNE1 transfer does not improve grouped validation reliably, so I won’t claim it. I’ll check the evaluator’s prediction-test contract and the released scripts’ assumptions before deciding whether to add further results.

Before settling on the KRAS residual model, I’ll check whether its correction strength or feature set can improve generalization against the exact alpha-1 comparator. I’ll evaluate the same small, predeclared ridge grid on shuffled and position-grouped folds for both KRAS directions.

The KRAS ridge-grid results suggest that sequence-only residual corrections may generalize better than the earlier sequence-plus-substitution model. I’ll inspect the complete fold metrics, then add held-out prediction output for the strongest robust configuration and rerun it against the exact alpha-1 comparator.

A sequence-only residual model improves over the exact ridge baseline for both KRAS assays across shuffled and position-held-out folds. I’ll implement that specific model with a baseline fallback, then rerun it as prediction-ready evidence before publishing an updated method.

The sequence-only residual model improves on the exact alpha-1 baseline in all three shuffled folds and position-grouped validation for both KRAS assays. I’ll publish this stronger predictor; it uses paired source scores when available and the official ridge baseline otherwise.

The cross-assay gains are strongest for TEM-1 and KRAS. I’ll also check whether simply tuning ridge regularization improves the comparator across the remaining assays, using shuffled and position-grouped folds before considering any new prediction claims.

The TEM-1 companion-score mapping is strong, but I have only tested a linear calibration. I’ll compare it with restrained nonlinear calibrations under shuffled and position-held-out splits to check whether assay-scale differences can be modeled more accurately without sacrificing generalization.

Nonlinear score calibration sharply reduces cross-validation error for both TEM-1 assays, but those calibration scores alone weren’t compared with the official ridge baseline.
